title: The Westminster Confession (Condensed)
subtitle: The Reformed tradition's most complete doctrinal statement, drafted by the Westminster Assembly (1643–1646) — condensed here chapter-group by chapter-group, with notes.
intro: While England fought its civil war, Parliament summoned over a hundred ministers and scholars to Westminster Abbey to reform the national church. They met more than a thousand times across the 1640s and produced the most carefully argued confession the Reformed tradition possesses, finished in 1646, along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. It became the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches across the world, was lightly adapted by Congregationalists, and — with baptism and church government revised — became the backbone of the Baptist confession of 1689. Whatever an American Protestant believes about God's sovereignty, Scripture, or the covenant, this document has usually shaped it somewhere upstream. The condensation below is a faithful paraphrase of the confession's thirty-three chapters in their own order; it is not the full text, which runs many times this length.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the confession's thirty-three chapters. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

Of Holy Scripture (ch. 1). Scripture is the written Word of God, given by inspiration, complete in what it teaches for salvation, and the final rule for faith and life. Its authority rests on God its author, not the church's approval; the Spirit persuades the reader of it; and every religious controversy is finally settled by the Spirit speaking in the Scriptures.

Of God, the Trinity, and His Decree (chs. 2–5). There is one living and true God — infinite, unchangeable, just, and good — in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. From eternity God freely ordained whatever comes to pass, yet so that he is not the author of sin, no violence is done to the will of the creature, and secondary causes stand. He created all things good and governs all things by his providence, down to the sparrow.

Of the Fall, the Covenant, and Christ the Mediator (chs. 6–8). Our first parents sinned; guilt and corruption descend to all their children; humanity is dead in sin and unable to convert itself. God condescended to deal with man by covenant — a covenant of works with Adam, and after the fall a covenant of grace, offering life through faith in Jesus Christ. Christ, truly God and truly man, is the one Mediator: prophet, priest, and king, who obeyed, suffered, rose, and intercedes, purchasing redemption for all whom the Father has given him.

Of Salvation Applied (chs. 9–18). The will, free by nature, is bound by sin until grace frees it. God effectually calls his elect — enlightening, renewing, and drawing them so that they come most freely. They are justified: declared righteous not for anything wrought in them but for Christ's obedience and satisfaction credited to them, received by faith alone, which is never alone. They are adopted as children, and sanctified — really and personally renewed, though imperfectly in this life, sin's remnants warring in them to the end. Saving faith feeds on the Word; repentance unto life turns from sin to God; good works, done in obedience, are faith's fruit and evidence, unable to earn anything and yet pleasing to God in Christ. Those God has accepted can neither totally nor finally fall away, though they may grievously sin, grieve the Spirit, and lose assurance for a season — and assurance itself, the confession insists, may be attained without extraordinary revelation, may be shaken, and may be revived.

Of the Law, Liberty, Worship, and the Sabbath (chs. 19–24). The moral law binds all people always, not as a covenant to be earned but as a rule of life; Christian liberty frees the conscience from the doctrines and commandments of men; God may be worshiped only as he has appointed; oaths are lawful when taken in truth; one day in seven is to be kept holy to the Lord.

Of the Church and the Sacraments (chs. 25–31). The catholic church, invisible, consists of the whole number of the elect; the visible church consists of all who profess the true religion together with their children, and outside it there is no ordinary possibility of salvation. Christ alone is its head. The communion of saints binds believers to Christ and to one another in gifts and graces. There are two sacraments, baptism — rightly administered to believers and to their children — and the Lord's Supper, in which worthy receivers really and spiritually feed on Christ, though the bread and wine remain what they are. Church censures exist to reclaim offenders and guard the table; synods and councils may err, and many have.

Of the Last Things (chs. 32–33). At death the righteous are received into glory and the wicked into torment; at the last day all shall rise, all shall be judged by Jesus Christ, and the righteous shall go into everlasting life and the wicked into everlasting punishment — an end appointed, the confession closes, both to deter all men from sin and to comfort the godly in their adversity.

annotations.phrase: the Spirit speaking in the Scriptures
annotations.note: The confession's opening chapter is its most influential. Written amid competing claims of church authority, inner light, and reason, it locates the final word in Scripture itself — and grounds Scripture's authority in God, not in the institution that canonized it. Chapter one has functioned ever since as Protestantism's working doctrine of the Bible.

annotations.phrase: no violence is done to the will of the creature
annotations.note: Westminster states the hard doctrine — God ordains whatsoever comes to pass — and immediately fences it: God is not the author of sin, and human willing remains real willing. Whether those two sentences can both be held is the standing argument between Reformed and Arminian believers; the confession's care in stating both is often missed by both sides' partisans. This platform files the question as second-order: it divides faithful churches, not the faith.

annotations.phrase: received by faith alone, which is never alone
annotations.note: The confession's summary of the Reformation's center: justification by faith apart from works, and a justifying faith that always produces works. Chapters eleven and sixteen together answer the oldest objection to grace — that it makes holiness optional — without surrendering the gift.

annotations.phrase: the backbone of the Baptist confession of 1689
annotations.note: The writer's own tradition took this document, revised its chapters on baptism and the church, and adopted the rest nearly whole. A Baptist reading Westminster is reading his family's older handwriting — which is exactly why it is condensed on this shelf beside the 1689.
